title: Throughput & Fallbacks: Dedicated vs Hosted cost/latency tradeoffs
summary: Deep dive on isolation strategies across Dedicated vs Hosted, noisy-neighbor mitigation, KV cache prefetch/eviction, batching windows and quantization choices. Decided to run a 2-week pilot: focused perf benchmarks (P95/P99), cost delta analysis, and a KV-prefetch pilot on dedicated capacity. Security questions captured for Private/VPC and KMS integration.

batching latency windows and dynamic batching
quantization (int8 vs int4) impact on perf

transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-12-02 15:00 UTC | Duration: 72 minutes | Recording: yes
Attendees: Alex Murphy (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Jon Park (Redwood Solutions), Tom Chen (BlueArc VP Eng), Leila Ramos (BlueArc Platform Eng), Samir Patel (BlueArc SRE), Nadia K. (BlueArc SecOps)

[00:00] Alex: hey everyone, thanks for joining. think we have about 70 minutes, want to get into the architecture tradeoffs between running on Dedicated nodes versus staying Hosted and how fallbacks and noisy neighbor stuff will affect your p95/p99s.
[00:18] Tom: yeah thank you. we've seen a few production incidents where latency spikes when a big batch job hits — that's our main worry, plus cost.
[00:30] Priya: got it. quick clarifying q, is your critical path mainly interactive chat flows or high-throughput embedding pipelines?
[00:40] Tom: mostly interactive — chat + short docs summarization with occasional bulk embeddings overnight. seq lengths avg 128 tokens but tails up to 1024 for some customers.
[00:55] Samir: and we have multi-tenant appservers backing different customers; we want isolation so Customer A's analytics job doesn't blow up latency for Customer B.
[01:08] Priya: ok great. so the tradeoff ladder — Dedicated gives you stronger isolation and more predictable throughput (you can reserve GPU pools), Hosted gives you elasticity and lower ops but you can see noisy-neighbor effects if capacity is tight.
[01:25] Leila: can you unpack noisy-neighbor? we've read about continuous batching and KV cache — how do those interact?
[01:34] Priya: yes. short version: long-running batched workloads can fill the batch windows and push latency up for small interactive requests. KV cache (we call prefix/KV caching here) reduces token work for repeated contexts but it needs memory and can be evicted under pressure. so if a big batch job evicts KV entries for interactive sessions, those sessions get cold-cache latencies.
[01:55] Nadia: is eviction a process we can tune? we have strict SLOs for customers in EU region, need consistent p99.
[02:03] Jon: eviction policy is tunable — LRU-ish plus priority pinning. on Dedicated you can fence capacity and reserve KV memory; on Hosted we can do soft reservation or prefer routes for higher tiers but can't guarantee hard isolation unless you buy dedicated pools.
[02:20] Tom: what about fallback routing? we'd rather keep service up and divert to a slightly cheaper/slower model than fail. is that supported?
[02:29] Alex: yes. Redwood supports routing policies: latency-first, cost-first, or hybrid. you can set automatic fallback to a compatible model variant (lower compute quantization or smaller architecture). we also have region fallback if a zone is constrained.
[02:43] Samir: we'd be worried about semantic drift when falling back to smaller models — can you control when to fall back?
[02:50] Priya: Absolutely. fallbacks can be gated by a confidence or eval metric; also you can define per-endpoint tolerances for hallucination risk. during the pilot we recommend capturing quality metrics alongside latency/cost so you can quantify delta.
[03:05] Tom: ok. let's talk numbers — what ballpark latency differences are we looking at for int8 vs int4 quant?
[03:13] Priya: anecdotal: int8 often gives ~15-30% faster token throughput with minimal quality loss for many models; int4 gives larger speedups but more variability depending on the model and compiler/kernel support. very model-dependent. we should benchmark your prompt distribution.
[03:30] Leila: and kernel selection — you mentioned automatic kernel selection. how stable is that?
[03:35] Jon: runtime picks kernels based on sequence length distribution and hardware — sometimes we pick a kernel that optimizes long sequences but penalizes short ones. we expose a knob to bias kernel selection for low-latency short requests.
[03:49] Tom: so for our use case (short interactive), you'd bias towards short-seq kernels even if it lowers peak throughput?
[03:55] Priya: yes, that's an explicit policy. you can also set per-tenant priorities so critical customers get pinned kernels and more KV memory.
[04:06] Nadia: on security — if we go Dedicated or Private, how does KMS/HSM integration work? we need to ensure keys never leave our control.
[04:14] Alex: for Private deployments we can integrate with your KMS (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, or bring-your-own HSM). for Dedicated we offer a customer-managed KMS option where keys are in your account and we use transient wrapping keys on our side. we'll include the integration diagram in the security pack.
[04:31] Nadia: and audit logs?
[04:33] Jon: full request-level audit logs available in Dedicated/Private. Hosted also provides logs but with different retention and redaction settings depending on plan.
[04:40] Leila: let's return to KV cache prefetching — can we warm the cache during a burst?
[04:46] Priya: yes — we have an API to pre-warm KV entries based on expected prefixes. also a background warm-up process during traffic spikes. important caveat: prefetching increases memory usage and potentially cost on Dedicated.
[04:59] Tom: how do you measure warm vs cold penalty?
[05:03] Priya: we capture delta in token generation time — typically cold can be 2-5x slower for the first few tokens because of recomputation. we'll put concrete numbers in the runbook with your traces.
[05:15] Samir: about batching windows — what's the sweet spot? we want low latency but also cost efficiency.
[05:21] Priya: there's a trade. small windows (10-30ms) favor latency but lower throughput efficiency; larger windows (50-200ms) increase throughput and reduce cost per token. Adaptive windows that shrink when queue depth is low work well. We can show your workload simulations.
[05:38] Tom: do you support dynamic batching that accounts for priority? like preempt small interactive requests?
[05:44] Jon: yes, we have priority preemption — small high-priority requests can cut the queue and be served with reserved slots. This is more straightforward on Dedicated where you can reserve slots. On Hosted it's available but best-effort.
[05:58] Leila: what about tail latency mitigation? P99 spikes are what keep us up at night.
[06:03] Priya: two approaches — first, increase isolation (dedicated pools) or reserved KV memory; second, run autoscaling with cold-start buffer and short warmup capacity. Also architectural: using a local prefix cache at your edge to serve very small repetitive requests.
[06:18] Tom: local prefix cache — would that sit in our infra?
[06:21] Priya: yes, an edge KV that stores top-K prefixes; reduces round-trip and token work. nice for repeated user greetings and templated prompts.
[06:30] Nadia: any operational complexity there? we don't want another system to manage.
[06:33] Alex: Redwood can manage it as part of Private deployment or give a simple containerized edge cache you run. We'll scope options in the pilot.
[06:45] Samir: pricing — give me a comparable number: if we move from Hosted to Dedicated with reserved pools, how much more would we commit monthly?
[06:53] Jon: rough numbers: Dedicated baseline for your 3-node pilot is about 2.5x the baseline hosted compute cost but gives 4-5x more predictable throughput and lower P99 variance. Exact depends on GPU types, quant and batching settings. We'll provide an itemized estimate.
[07:09] Tom: 2.5x is big — can we mix modes? like Dedicated for interactive tiered traffic and Hosted for bulk embeddings?
[07:16] Priya: absolutely. hybrid routing is common: high-priority interactive endpoints pinned to Dedicated, bulk jobs routed to Hosted where cost is cheaper and latency less critical.
[07:25] Leila: how do you handle model version rollouts across hybrid? we need consistent inference across both modes.
[07:31] Jon: we support pinned model versions and model variant mapping. you can pin exact weights and quant settings for Dedicated and a fallback variant for Hosted; Redwood Console shows consistency diffs and a canary rollout feature.
[07:45] Tom: okay good. for our pilot can we test two axes: (1) isolation (dedicated vs hosted) and (2) quantization modes int8 vs int4 — measure P95/P99 and embedding cosine delta?
[07:55] Priya: yes, that's exactly the pilot plan we'd recommend. also capture token-level cost.
[08:02] Nadia: about regulatory — we need EU data residency and SOC2. if we go Hosted, can you guarantee EU-only processing?
[08:09] Alex: we have EU-region hosted endpoints and can set routing to region-only. For strict compliance, Private deployment or Dedicated in your cloud account is more controlled. We'll include SOC2 docs.
[08:21] Tom: sample pilot timeline?
[08:23] Jon: propose: week 1 — instrument traces and upload data; week 2 — spin Dedicated pilot nodes and run baseline benchmark; week 3 — run quantization/kv/batching experiments; week 4 — analyze results and decision meeting.
[08:36] Leila: that sounds good. what metrics will you deliver?
[08:40] Priya: P50/P95/P99 latency, token/sec, cost per 1k tokens, embedding cosine drift, cache hit rate, eviction rate, kernel selection logs, and per-request trace IDs for correlation.
[08:55] Samir: will you give us raw traces back? we need them for our SRE postmortem tooling.
[08:59] Jon: yes, sanitized traces will be shared; we can also run benchmarks in your account for maximum fidelity.
[09:08] Tom: any gotchas we should be aware of?
[09:11] Priya: watch out for sequence-length skew — if your long-tail is heavy, some kernels and batching choices can blow up memory; also some int4 paths can cause dequantization noise that affects hallucinations in summarization.
[09:24] Leila: if we see quality regressions on int4, can we tuning quantization per-layer or do we have to revert globally?
[09:30] Priya: we have per-layer and mixed-precision options for some model families, but it depends on model format. We'll test per-layer quant and report.
[09:40] Nadia: about network egress and VPC peering — firewall changes often take a week. what's needed from our side?
[09:46] Alex: we'll provide IP ranges and minimal port list. Leila said she'll share the firewall owner; we can align on a pre-approved list to speed up connectivity.
[09:56] Tom: curious about fallback semantics: if a Dedicated node is saturated, do you queue requests or divert immediately?
[10:02] Jon: configurable. you can set a soft queue with timeouts or immediate diversion to fallback model/host. For interactive we often recommend short timeout (200-400ms) then failover to a smaller model or Hosted.
[10:16] Samir: does failover cause duplicate billing if both paths execute?
[10:20] Alex: we have dedupe semantics — we avoid double-charge for successful request execution; partial retries are billed pro-rata. We'll include billing examples.
[10:30] Leila: ok let's document decision points for pilot config.
[10:33] Priya: I'll capture recommended defaults: Dedicated pool with 3 GPUs, reserve 20% KV memory for interactive tenants, priority preemption enabled, batching window adaptive starting at 30ms, quant int8 default with int4 experiments.
[10:51] Tom: perfect. any questions from the customer side we missed?
[10:54] Nadia: one on monitoring — can we get token-level cost broken down by API key/client?
[10:59] Jon: yes per-token breakdown in Console; we'll enable retention for 90 days for the pilot.
[11:06] Tom: last q — how do you validate semantic parity when moving between variants? is there a tooling?
[11:12] Priya: Redwood Optimize has an eval harness where you run prompt suites and compute metrics like ROUGE/EM/embedding drift. We'll run your prompt set and include those diffs.
[11:24] Alex: ok wrapping: we'll send the security pack, perf runbook, and cost estimate. Pilot timeline as Jon said. Anything else?
[11:33] Tom: sounds good. thanks all.
[11:36] Alex: thanks everyone, follow-up emails will include next steps and action items.

END OF TRANSCRIPT
